case_study_insert.main_stem: Goldenfields Dairies (GFD) is a private limited company in the dairy-processing sector, based in the Waikato region and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, it supplies branded yoghurt to national supermarkets and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. GFD plans to invest $960,000 in a new yoghurt-filling line with recyclable tubs, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $16, and produces 120,000 units a year. GFD faces rising milk-spillage waste of 6% of intake and absenteeism of 8% among its production staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The dairy line filled 28,500 tubs last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 24 a month. Average delivery to supermarkets was 2.8 days. A survey of 750 shoppers found 61% would pay $0.30 more for a recyclable tub, and 48% check the origin label. Milk-spillage waste stood at 6% of intake. A skills audit shows 15 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Goldenfields Dairies as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Agri-Food Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing the cost of the $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $13.40 to $14.27 an hour, lifting dairy-processing payroll costs. (3) Wholesale feed and packaging input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on branded yoghurt grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: GFD is funding part of its $960,000 yoghurt-filling line with a $600,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GFD of using the $360,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or mandatory repayment, so GFD protects the cash flow needed to cover fixed costs of $360,000 a year while it services the existing $600,000 loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in feed and packaging costs, helping GFD hold its $16 selling price and supply national supermarkets without passing costs on.

Point 2: Using $360,000 retained profit keeps Priya Nandakumar's ownership intact and avoids further collateral risk. The new $960,000 filling line cannot be threatened by a bank recall if demand falls short, and the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers willing to pay $0.30 more for a recyclable tub gives the family-owned business confidence to fund the launch from its own resources rather than increase borrowing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GFD's financing decision and dairy operations.

questions.question_text: GFD is launching its new recyclable-tub yoghurt range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should GFD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: TV gives GFD mass reach and can show the new yoghurt-filling line and recyclable tubs to millions, building awareness across the national supermarket chains it supplies. The drawback is cost: airtime and production are expensive for a business with $360,000 fixed costs and a $600,000 loan, and much of the audience will never see GFD's tubs on a shelf, so spend is wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and reaches GFD's regional catchment, and short messages can announce the recyclable tub cheaply. Its limit is that audio cannot show the tub or the 61% of 750 shoppers who would pay $0.30 more, and the range is sold nationally, so a local audience cannot generate the 120,000-unit volume the $960,000 line needs.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can show the recyclable tub directly and reach the 48% of surveyed shoppers who check the origin label, with engagement measured against the 28,500 tubs filled last quarter. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on credible partners, but cost per reached shopper is low and the message can be targeted at the shoppers already identified in GFD's research.

Recommendation: GFD should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by modest in-store supermarket displays. It reaches the exact segment in the survey, displays the recyclable tub that radio cannot, and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-person firm funding a $960,000 line; radio is rejected as too narrow for national distribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to GFD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GFD with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: GFD's absenteeism has reached 8% and waste is 6% of intake under its democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for GFD of involving its workforce of 60 in decisions about the new filling line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 60 employees suggest how the new yoghurt-filling line is run, raising job satisfaction and commitment. Workers who help set filler routines are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism that currently disrupts the 28,500-tub quarterly output and helps protect delivery times of 2.8 days to supermarkets.

Point 2: Involvement draws on the knowledge of operators who handle milk daily, so they can propose ways to cut the 6% spillage waste and the 2.2% defect rate. Higher morale also lowers the need to retrain the 15 of 60 staff still missing on-the-job training at $780 each, protecting the $16 selling price and contribution while the $960,000 line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GFD's absenteeism, waste, output and expansion.

questions.question_text: GFD must train 15 of 60 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should GFD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the filler is specific to GFD's own machines and hygiene routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 15 trainees productive during the 28,500-tub quarter. It can directly address the 6% spillage waste and the 2.2% defect rate because supervisors correct practice immediately. Drawbacks are that busy operators have less time to teach, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for supermarket audits.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $780 per employee costs 15 × $780 = $11,700, small beside the $960,000 investment. It gives structured dairy-hygiene skills and a recognised certificate, useful when supplying national supermarkets. However, it removes 15 of 60 staff from the line during production, risking longer than 2.8-day deliveries, and generic content will still need on-site adaptation to GFD's filler.

Decision: GFD should choose on-the-job training first, with short certified college modules later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids worsening output while 8% absenteeism already stretches a workforce of 60. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost shifts and $11,700 fee would hit the 28,500-tub operation and generic teaching would not cover the new filler's exact settings. A pilot on one shift should compare the 2.2% defect rate and 6% waste before GFD spends $11,700 on all 15 staff.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GFD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of GFD.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GFD's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $8.00) = $360,000 ÷ $8.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $8.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GFD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units gives GFD a margin of safety of 75,000 units, showing how far sales could fall before losses begin and guiding use of the $960,000 filling line.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets managers test pricing: cutting the $16.00 price by $1 to $15.00 leaves $7.00 contribution, so they can judge whether extra supermarket volume would still cover the $360,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $360,000 and contribution of $8.00 helps set the volume needed to service the $600,000 bank loan, checking the new line can meet repayments before GFD commits further capital.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $360,000 ÷ 120,000 units = $3.00 plus $8.00 = $11.00 a tub, across quarters to spot the 6% spillage waste and assess whether to renegotiate the $8.00 variable cost amid 9.8% input inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 75,000-unit safety margin versus 120,000-unit output; discount pricing from $16.00 against $8.00 contribution; loan-service volume for the $600,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.00 to tackle 6% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GFD's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GFD's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.75 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.06 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $315,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $140,000 + $80,000 = $350,000. For 2024, $315,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.75 and ($315,000 − $150,000) ÷ $180,000 = $165,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.92. For 2025, $350,000 ÷ $170,000 = 2.06 and ($350,000 − $130,000) ÷ $170,000 = $220,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.29.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened clearly. The first ratio rose from 1.75 to 2.06 because current assets grew from $315,000 to $350,000 while current liabilities fell from $180,000 to $170,000. The second measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.92 to 1.29, so GFD can now cover short-term debts without relying on selling $130,000 of yoghurt stock — important while it services a $600,000 loan and funds a $960,000 line. The reservation is trade receivables, up from $110,000 to $140,000, which tie up cash; if supermarkets pay late, the improvement could reverse quickly, and inventories have fallen to $130,000, so stock cover for promotions should be watched.

Conclusion: GFD's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the gain does not depend on stock, leaving a safer short-term position. The main residual risk is higher receivables, so GFD should tighten credit control as the expansion proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: GFD is considering switching its whole range to recyclable tubs. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GFD of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable tubs match the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.30 more and the 48% who check the origin label, letting GFD charge a premium that protects the $8.00 contribution per unit even as feed and packaging costs rise 9.8%. The switch also strengthens the brand with national supermarkets and supports the $960,000 filling-line investment.

Disadvantage: Recyclable materials usually cost more than standard plastic, which would raise the $8.00 variable cost per unit unless the $0.30 premium is accepted on every tub. The insert gives no figure for the extra material cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified. Any sealing failure would also lift the current 2.2% defect rate and worsen the 6% spillage waste before the new line stabilises, squeezing returns on the launch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GFD's research, costs and defect data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in feed and packaging input costs will affect GFD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If GFD's $600,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates may also make future borrowing for the $960,000 expansion dearer and slightly dampen the 4.2% growth in branded yoghurt spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $14.27 an hour): GFD's workforce of 60 includes hourly-paid production and packing staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 2,000 tubs per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 8% absenteeism and training the 15 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (9.8%): Feed and packaging feed the $8.00 variable cost on every tub. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the entire $8.00 were exposed, 9.8% × $8.00 = $0.784, about $0.78 a tub, and at 120,000 units that is roughly $94,080 a year (120,000 × $0.784). A smaller exposed share would still erode the $8.00 contribution each time GFD sells a tub, and the effect repeats with every unit.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across 120,000 tubs and directly attacks the contribution that funds the $600,000 loan and $960,000 line, whereas the interest rise costs $4,500 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 2,000 tubs per worker. GFD should cut the 6% waste and seek the $0.30 recyclable-tub premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GFD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GFD's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
